question: What are data classes in Kotlin and what does the compiler generate?
answer:
A `data class` exists to hold data, and the compiler generates its equality, printing, copying and destructuring for you.

• `equals()` / `hashCode()` from the primary-constructor properties ONLY — a property declared in the class body is ignored by both.
• `toString()` like `User(id=1, name=Alice)`.
• `copy(...)` — a new instance with selected fields replaced.
• `componentN()` operators, which is what makes destructuring work.

Requirements: at least one primary-constructor parameter, and every one of them must be `val` or `var`. A data class cannot be `abstract`, `open`, `sealed` or `inner`, though it may extend a non-data class.

Two modern points. `data object` gives a singleton a readable `toString()` and a stable `equals`, which is why sealed hierarchies now write `data object Loading`. And a private constructor no longer leaks silently through `copy()`: since Kotlin 2.0.20 that combination is deprecated — opt in with `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` or stop using a data class there.

Two traps to name in an interview: `copy()` is shallow, so nested mutable objects stay shared, and structural equality over a mutable property will change an object's hashCode after it has been put in a HashSet.

question: What are sealed classes / sealed interfaces in Kotlin?
answer:
A sealed class/interface restricts who can extend it: only classes declared in the SAME module + same package (sealed class) or same module (sealed interface) can subclass.

This enables:
• Exhaustive `when` — no `else` branch needed; if you add a new subtype, the compiler errors at every existing `when`.
• Algebraic-data-type modeling — express finite alternatives like `Result`, screen state, parser tokens.
• Library API design — control extensibility while still using inheritance.

Sealed types are reference types; the JVM treats them as ordinary classes. Use `data class` or `data object` subclasses for value semantics.

question: What is the difference between class, object, and companion object in Kotlin?
answer:
`object` declares a singleton, `companion object` is a singleton bound to a class, and `class` is the ordinary instantiable declaration.

• `class` — instantiated with `Foo()`; every instance is separate.
• `object` — a named singleton. The compiler creates exactly one instance, initialized lazily and thread-safely on first access, reachable as `MyService.action()`.
• `companion object` — a singleton tied to an enclosing class, holding the static-like members Kotlin has no `static` keyword for: factories, constants, `operator invoke`. Reached through the class name (`User.create(...)`).

Objects can implement interfaces and extend one class, which is what makes them useful as stateless strategies, comparators and DI entry points. An anonymous `object : Listener { ... }` expression is Kotlin's version of a Java anonymous class, and unlike a named object it may capture surrounding state.

Two traps: a companion member is NOT a JVM static, so Java callers need `@JvmStatic`; and a top-level `object` lives for the whole process, which makes holding mutable state or an Android Context in one a classic leak. For genuine compile-time constants use `const val` at top level or inside an object.

question: What are extension functions and properties in Kotlin?
answer:
Extensions add functions or properties to existing types without modifying their source. Resolved STATICALLY — the compiler picks the extension based on the static type of the receiver.

• `fun String.titleCase(): String = ...` — extension function.
• `val String.firstLetter: Char get() = first()` — extension property (no backing field; computed only).
• Member functions win over extensions with the same signature on the same type.
• Extensions don't override virtual methods — they're static dispatch.

Idiomatic uses: utility helpers (`Date.toIsoString()`), domain DSLs, view-binding helpers in Android, ergonomic API on third-party types.

question: What are scope functions (let, run, with, apply, also)?
answer:
Scope functions run a lambda in the context of an object, and they differ on two axes: how the object is referenced (`it` vs `this`) and what the lambda returns (the object itself vs the lambda result).

• `let` — refer as `it`, returns lambda result. Common for null-safe transforms.
• `run` — refer as `this`, returns lambda result. For computing on an object.
• `with` — refer as `this`, returns lambda result. Like run, but as standalone function.
• `apply` — refer as `this`, returns the object. For configuring an object after construction.
• `also` — refer as `it`, returns the object. For side effects (logging, validation) without breaking a chain.

Guideline: pick the pair (`it`/`this`, value/object) that makes the call site cleanest. Don't nest scope functions deeply.

question: Kotlin classes are final by default — how do `open class`, `abstract class` and `interface` differ?
answer:
Kotlin makes every class final by default, so `open`, `abstract` and `interface` are three different ways of opting into extension.

• `class` — final. Neither the class nor its members can be extended or overridden unless marked `open`.
• `open class` — subclassable, but only members that are themselves `open` can be overridden, and each override must carry the `override` keyword (it is mandatory in Kotlin, unlike Java's optional `@Override`).
• `abstract class` — cannot be instantiated. It may hold state through constructor properties and mix abstract with concrete members. Single inheritance, and `abstract` already implies `open`.
• `interface` — no backing fields, therefore no stored state, but it may declare abstract members, default implementations and computed properties. A class can implement many.

Kotlin's bias toward final-by-default is deliberate: the author must opt into extensibility, which heads off fragile-base-class problems.

The Kotlin-specific spellings are worth naming: a single colon covers both `extends` and `implements` (`class Service : Repository(), Logger`), the superclass constructor is called right there in that clause, and `super<A>.greet()` disambiguates when two interfaces supply the same default implementation.

Choose an interface for a contract or capability, an abstract class when subtypes must share state, a data class for a value type, and `sealed` when the set of subtypes is closed and you want `when` to stay exhaustive.

question: Which visibility modifiers does Kotlin have, and what does `internal` actually cover?
answer:
Kotlin declarations are `public` unless you say otherwise, and its extra level is `internal`, meaning visible everywhere inside the same compilation module.

• `public` — the default. Nothing is package-private by accident the way it is in Java.
• `private` — on a top-level declaration, visible inside that FILE; on a member, inside the class only.
• `protected` — the class and its subclasses. Unlike Java it does NOT leak to the rest of the package.
• `internal` — the whole module, where a module is one set of sources compiled together: a Gradle source set, a Maven module, an IntelliJ module.

Things worth knowing about `internal` in an Android multi-module build:
• It is the tool for keeping a module's implementation types out of its public surface — the DTOs, mappers and DAOs that only exist so the repository can work.
• Pair it with Gradle's `implementation` versus `api` configurations: `internal` stops other modules from referencing the type, `implementation` stops them from even seeing the dependency.
• The unit-test source set of the same module can see `internal` declarations, which is why a class does not have to be public just to be tested.
• On the JVM the compiler mangles the names, so `internal` is enforced for Kotlin callers but a determined Java caller can still reach it.

Visibility applies to constructors too: `class Config private constructor(...)` with a companion factory is the standard way to control how a type is created.

question: In what order do the primary constructor, property initializers, `init` blocks and a secondary constructor run?
answer:
Initialization runs top to bottom through the class body, and a secondary constructor's own body is the last thing to execute.

The exact sequence for `SecondaryCtor()` on a subclass:
1. The arguments of the secondary constructor are evaluated and it delegates, with `this(...)` to the primary constructor or with `super(...)` to the base class.
2. The base class is fully initialized before anything in the subclass.
3. The primary constructor binds its parameters.
4. Property initializers and `init { }` blocks run interleaved, in the order they are written in the class body — an `init` block cannot read a property declared below it.
5. The secondary constructor's own body runs, so it sees a fully initialized object.

Two consequences interviewers push on:
• Because the base class finishes first, calling an `open` member from a base-class `init` block or property initializer runs the subclass override while the subclass's own properties are still null or zero. Never call an overridable member during construction.
• A secondary constructor is usually the wrong tool in Kotlin. Default and named arguments cover most of what overloaded constructors do in Java, and a companion factory function covers the rest with a name that says what it builds.

The `constructor` keyword itself is optional on the primary constructor, needed only when it carries an annotation or a visibility modifier.

question: You chain `map` and `filter` over a list. When does inserting `asSequence()` actually make it faster?
answer:
A collection chain materializes a new list at every step, while a sequence pushes one element through the whole chain before touching the next.

How a sequence behaves:
• Intermediate operations (`map`, `filter`, `take`, `flatMap`) are lazy and build a pipeline; nothing runs until a terminal operation such as `toList`, `first`, `sum`, `count` or `forEach` pulls values through it.
• Because evaluation is element-wise, a short-circuiting terminal stops the whole pipeline early: `asSequence().map(::expensive).first { it.valid }` may call `expensive` once instead of a million times.
• `generateSequence` and `sequence { yield(...) }` let the source itself be infinite or produced on demand.

When it pays off:
• A large collection with several chained steps — you skip one intermediate list per step, which is the allocation and the GC pressure people actually measure.
• Any chain that ends in a short-circuit, or a source that is expensive to produce.

When it does not:
• Small collections, the common case in UI code. A few dozen elements through two operations is faster eagerly, because each sequence step costs an iterator and a lambda call per element.
• A single operation. `list.map { }.asSequence()` helps nobody.

Two behaviours to remember: the interleaved order means side effects inside `map` no longer happen in one batch, and some sequences are single-use, so collecting one twice throws.

question: What does `class LoggingRepo(private val inner: Repo) : Repo by inner` generate, and where does that delegation stop helping?
answer:
Interface delegation makes the compiler generate every method of the interface as a one-line forwarding call to the given object, so a decorator costs one line instead of twenty.

• `: Repo by inner` implements the whole `Repo` surface by calling `inner`. Any member you also declare yourself wins over the generated forwarder, which is exactly how you intercept one method and pass the rest through.
• It is composition, not inheritance: the wrapped type does not have to be `open`, and you never inherit state you did not want.
• Useful for logging, caching, retry, feature-flag switches, and for test doubles that override one call on top of a real implementation.

The trap is that the delegate has no idea it is being wrapped. Calls that `inner` makes to its own methods stay inside `inner`, so if `Repo.refresh()` internally calls `load()`, your override of `load()` is not involved. There is no virtual dispatch back into the wrapper the way there would be with subclassing — an argument in favour of delegation for isolation and against it when you expected an override to apply everywhere.

Two smaller details: the object is captured once when the wrapper is constructed, so reassigning the original variable later changes nothing, and the value passed to `by` is only accessible as a property if you declare it as one in the constructor.

question: When can you pass a lambda where an interface is expected in Kotlin?
answer:
A lambda converts to an interface only when that interface comes from Java with a single abstract method, or is a Kotlin interface declared `fun interface`.

• Java single-abstract-method types get SAM conversion for free: `Runnable { }`, `view.setOnClickListener { }`, an OkHttp `Interceptor`.
• A plain Kotlin interface with one method does NOT accept a lambda. Add the `fun` keyword — `fun interface Validator { fun check(s: String): Boolean }` — and it does, and you also get the SAM-constructor form `Validator { it.isNotBlank() }`.
• For anything with more than one method, use an anonymous object: `object : AnimatorListener { ... }`, which unlike a lambda can hold state and override several members.

The design question behind this is whether you want an interface at all. In Kotlin the default is a function type — `onClick: () -> Unit`, `validate: (String) -> Boolean` — because callers pass a lambda, a method reference or a stored variable with no ceremony, and no extra type has to be documented. Choose `fun interface` when you need a name that carries meaning, when Java callers must implement it, or when the type needs default methods and extra members alongside the abstract one.

One behavioural difference worth stating: a bare `return` inside a lambda passed to a non-inline function is not allowed, and inside an anonymous object's method it returns from that method only.

question: How do you make `+`, `[]` and `in` work on a type of your own?
answer:
Kotlin maps each operator to one fixed function name, and marking that function `operator` is the entire opt-in.

The mapping people are expected to know:
• `a + b` to `plus`, and likewise `minus`, `times`, `div`, `rem`, `unaryMinus`.
• `a[i]` to `get`, `a[i] = v` to `set`.
• `a(x)` to `invoke` — the reason a companion object with `operator fun invoke` lets `Factory(...)` look like a constructor.
• `x in a` to `contains`, `a..b` to `rangeTo`, `a < b` to `compareTo` through `Comparable`.
• `for (x in a)` to `iterator`, and destructuring to `component1`, `component2` and so on.

Rules: the names are fixed, you cannot invent new operators, precedence is not configurable, and an operator can be declared as an extension on a type you do not own. `a += b` resolves to `plusAssign` when it exists and to `a = a.plus(b)` when it does not — declaring both on a mutable receiver is an ambiguity error, so give an immutable type `plus` and a mutable one `plusAssign`.

The judgement half of the answer: operators are right for values with real arithmetic or set semantics — money, durations, vectors, matrices, geometry — and for DSL builders. They are wrong when the symbol hides an effect a reader cannot guess, such as `+` that writes to a database.
